as_told.title: Robertson Panel's secret recommendations to debunk, detect and track

tellings.quote: The Panel's concept of a broad educational program integrating efforts of all concerned agencies was that it should have two major aims: training and "debunking."

The "debunking" aim would result in reduction in public interest in "flying saucers" which today evokes a strong psychological reaction. This education could be accomplished by mass media such as television, motion pictures, and popular articles.
That the national security agencies take immediate steps to strip the Unidentified Flying Objects of the special status they have been given and the aura of mystery they have unfortunately acquired;

tellings.page: Part II, Unofficial Investigating Groups, pp. 1416-1417
tellings.quote: The Panel took cognizance of the existence of such groups as the "Civilian Flying Saucer Investigators" (Los Angeles) and the "Aerial Phenomena Research Organization (Wisconsin). It was believed that such organizations should be watched because of their potentially great influence on mass thinking if widespread sightings should occur. The apparent irresponsibility and the possible use of such groups for subversive purposes should be kept in mind.

plain: In January 1953 the CIA brought together a group of scientists, later called the Robertson panel, to look at UFO reports, and according to the tellers it advised the government to talk the subject down in public and to keep an eye on civilian UFO groups. A guest named Karl Nell tells Michels that declassified papers show the panel decided the government should "debunk this topic" to misdirect the public and should "infiltrate" the organizations. A Senate staffer named Kurt McConnell says on the show that the panel made its recommendations in secret, one of them being that the government should be out "debunking" the existence of the objects. He also says it urged ways to detect and track them, names Howard P. Robertson, after whom the panel is named, and Luis Alvarez, and dates it to 1952 and 1953. The record dates the panel's meetings to 14 to 18 January 1953 and its report, from the CIA's Office of Scientific Intelligence, to 16 February 1953. The report itself calls for an education program with two aims, "training and 'debunking'," and says debunking "would result in reduction in public interest in 'flying saucers'" through television, films and popular articles. It also asks the security agencies to "strip the Unidentified Flying Objects of the special status they have been given and the aura of mystery" they had picked up. On civilian groups, it names the "Civilian Flying Saucer Investigators" of Los Angeles and the "Aerial Phenomena Research Organization" of Wisconsin and says such groups "should be watched" because of their possible influence on mass thinking, and that their "possible use... for subversive purposes should be kept in mind". So the report states the debunking aim outright, which is unusually direct, while the step from watching the groups to infiltrating them is the tellers' own reading, one the released text neither confirms nor rules out. If they read it rightly, the government's public skepticism about UFOs started as deliberate policy.

discussion.by: Report of Meetings of Scientific Advisory Panel on Unidentified Flying Objects (Robertson Panel), 14-18 January 1953
discussion.text: The tellers do not say which of the panel's papers they mean; if it is the minutes and report read here (the declassified text printed as Appendix U of the Condon report), the panel names the "Civilian Flying Saucer Investigators" and the "Aerial Phenomena Research Organization" and says such organizations "should be watched because of their potentially great influence on mass thinking" and that "the possible use of such groups for subversive purposes should be kept in mind", an official recommendation to keep watch on named civilian groups. The step from watched to infiltrated is the tellers' reading, which the report as released neither confirms nor excludes. As context, not as evidence: how a watch was to be kept is the kind of thing such minutes rarely set down.
